1:
Robertson takes the word for the look, atenisas, as more than formality: Paul may have had weak eyes, but the earnest gaze was probably to see whether he recognised faces from the body that had tried Stephen, and to which he apparently once belonged. Ellicott puts the interval at a quarter of a century since Paul stood there among Stephen's accusers; some of the faces were probably the same, and the Gazith, or Hall of Meeting on the south side of the Temple, with its circular benches, must have remained what it was. Barnes finds a second motive in what follows — Paul was arraigned before them and would naturally try to make out the character of his judges, and the result shows he was gauging the proportion of Pharisees and Sadducees he would appeal to five verses later. Gill reads the look outward rather than inward: fastening his eyes on them, looking wistly and intently, he discovered a modest cheerfulness and a becoming boldness, as one not conscious of any guilt and well assured of the goodness of his cause. Henry sets the scene against Stephen's. When Stephen was brought they thought to face him down and could not; now Paul thought to face them down and could not, such was their wicked impudence.

The claim itself turns on a verb that is not the ordinary one for living. Ellicott notes that it means literally I have used my citizenship, though it had lost that sharply defined sense and come to cover the whole course of a man's social conduct, so that my mode of life has been in all good conscience would be the nearest English. Robertson keeps the political colour and quotes Rackham — he had lived as God's citizen, as a member of God's commonwealth — with the dative marking how God looked at it. On the noun he observes that suneidesis is literally joint-knowledge, meaning consciousness of one's own thoughts, then of the distinction between right and wrong; but conscience is not an infallible guide and acts according to the light that it has. Ellicott agrees and draws the practical edge: it requires illumination, so each man needs to pray for light, yet it is never right to act against its dictates, and the objectively better course is subjectively the worse unless the man in his heart believes it better. Barnes states the corollary flatly: being conscientious does not prove a man right, or innocent.

How much of his life the claim covers is disputed. Clarke takes it whole: Paul was a Jew from principle and became a Christian because God persuaded his conscience that it was right, so that there was no part of his religious life in which he acted as a dishonest or hypocritical man. Wesley narrows it, holding that Paul speaks chiefly of the time since he became a Christian, since none questioned him concerning what he had been before — though even in his unconverted state, and in an error, he had acted from conscience. Henry inclines the same way and hears an answer to the charge of desertion: all the time in which you have looked upon me as an apostate and an enemy to your church, I have lived in all good conscience before God. Robertson grants that the claim seems to lack tact and sits uneasily beside Paul calling himself the chief of sinners, but reads it as a pointed disclaimer against the charge that he is a renegade Jew, an opposer of the law, the people and the temple, brevity forcing a whole speech into one sentence. Calvin sees a deliberate opening move: Paul means to mollify their nettled minds that he may the better be heard, and calls them brethren not because they deserve it but to testify that he is not the cause of the breach of friendship.
2:
The court's president is hard to place. Barnes identifies him as Ananias the son of Nebedinus, sent bound to Rome by Quadratus and dismissed through the intercession of the younger Agrippa, but not restored: Jonathan succeeded him, and when Jonathan's admonitions grew troublesome Felix persuaded his friend Doras to bring assassins upon him, who came into the city as if to worship, with daggers under their garments. The office then stood vacant until Agrippa appointed Ismael the son of Fabi, and Barnes places this hearing in that gap, with Ananias, the last man to have held the office, discharging its duties by common consent. On that reading Luke calls him high priest as the Jews would, and Paul's word two verses later is strictly true. Robertson dates the appointment differently, from Herod king of Chalcis in A.D. 48 to 59, with the summons to Rome in 52 on a charge of rapine and cruelty brought by the Samaritans, from which Page says he was honourably acquitted; high priest or not, he was a man of bad character. Clarke reports Krebs proving that acquittal and a restoration to the high priesthood. Calvin, working through the Antiquities and the Wars, cannot reconcile the succession at all, and conjectures that Ananias, excepting the title of honour almost chief in the order, held the room during the interval Josephus leaves void.

Ellicott finds the motive for the blow in a contrast. The son of Nebedaeus was conspicuous for cruelty and injustice, and the assertion of a life so unlike his own seemed almost a personal insult; he fitted the cap, and raged with a brutality Ellicott likens to Jeffreys' treatment of Baxter. Barnes puts it more plainly: their feelings had been excited to the utmost, they regarded Paul as an apostate, and could not bear his declaring so coolly that all his conduct had been under a good conscience. Robertson marks the illegality, quoting Knowling that the act was illegal and peculiarly offensive to a Jew at the hands of a Jew, but does not spare Paul either: more self-control might have served him better, and smiting the mouth is a peculiarly irritating offence, which gives point to Christ's command about the other cheek. The retort throws the verb straight back; Robertson observes that Paul puts smite first in the sentence for strong emphasis, and that the opening and thou expresses indignation. Whited wall, Barnes says, is proverbial for a hypocrite; he sets beside it Seneca on men sordid, base, and like their walls adorned only externally.

Whether the words were a curse divides them. Gill allows both readings, a prophecy of judgment or an imprecation, since may God smite thee is a recognised form of cursing and the future is often used for the imperative; but the instance is not to be drawn into example. Barnes denies the imprecation outright: it is a prediction, and a strong conviction that a man so hypocritical and unjust could not escape the vengeance of God. Calvin makes it neither curse nor outburst but a reprehension joined with the denouncing of a punishment, and meets the objection from the other cheek by distinguishing patience from silence — Christ bridles the desire of revenge, he does not require a silence whereby the frowardness of the wicked may be nourished, so that a sharp accusation proceeding from a quiet mind does not pass the bounds he set. Ellicott concedes more, taking the utterance by Paul's own confession as a hasty indignation recalled after a moment's reflection, yet actually a prophecy. On the fulfilment they agree. Wesley dates it about five years after, the house reduced to ashes in a tumult begun by his own son, Ananias besieged in the royal palace; Barnes has him killed with his brother Hezekiah when the robbers under Manahem held the city; both have him dragged from the aqueduct where he had hidden.
4:
Gill takes those that stood by for either the members of the council nearest Paul or the high priest's servants, leaning to the servants, since these stand whereas the court sat. Their protest, Robertson says, rests on the office rather than the man: Ananias was God's representative in spite of his bad character, and to revile him was a charge of irreverence, for the office called for respect. Barnes finds the appeal strange in their mouths, since they knew he was not the high priest; though he grants that Ananias stood in his place, and that they might have pretended respect was due to the office. Calvin turns the question round. Why do they not rather blame Ananias, who had quite forgotten all modesty and broken out into violence and stripes after a barbarous manner? It is a marked thing among hypocrites, he says, that they look narrowly into other men's faults and wink at their own, and the pride is coupled with tyranny, so that subjects may do nothing while rulers do whatever they will.

Ellicott sets out three readings and chooses among them. Either Paul literally did not know who had given the order, from defective sight or because the high priest was not sitting as president, and took it for a subordinate member; or the words were an ironical protest against an appointment improperly made; or I wist not stands for I did not consider, and the sentence is an apologetic recantation of words uttered in full knowledge. The first he judges by far the most probable, since the solemn sneer the second requires is at variance with Paul's character, and the third puts a greater strain on the words than they will bear. Barnes runs the same field and rejects both the irony and the apology, the latter because Paul evidently did not intend to retract; but thinks simple ignorance improbable too, since the presiding officer could hardly be unknown to the accused. His own solution is the vacancy: Paul did not acknowledge him as high priest, that not being truly his character, and had the office been really his, even manifest injustice would not have drawn such language. Clarke takes the plainest sense: the priesthood was no longer in succession but bought and sold, the Romans putting down one and raising another as policy dictated, so a man long absent might well not know the president from the sagan or a deputy.

What the answer concedes is disputed. Robertson thinks Paul at once recognises the justice of the point made against him and confesses his fault, the rebuke being deserved; he adds that Jesus, smitten on the cheek, did not threaten, but did protest and did not turn the other. Clarke denies any concession at all: Paul states two facts, that he did not know the man and that a ruler should be reverenced, but he neither recalled his words nor made apology, having committed no trespass and acknowledging none. Calvin, subscribing to Augustine, reads a taunting excuse, and defends the irony by dividing the figure in two, one sort covered with subtilty and meaning to deceive, another which so notes the thing in hand that it pricks the sorer, and only the first is unbecoming in a servant of Christ; the sense being that he acknowledges nothing in this man which belongs to the priest. Wesley hears something else again, that Paul did not advert to it in the prophetic transport of his mind, and observes that he does not say the transport came from the Spirit, knowing they could not bear it, but softens them with brethren and justifies their reproof out of Moses. Ellicott notes that the text quoted is one of those where Elohim is used of earthly rulers, and that the principle behind it governed the apostle throughout: Christianity was a great revolution, but its people were not revolutionists.
6:
Barnes supposes Paul read the room from old acquaintance: he had been brought up in Jerusalem and once commissioned by this body, though fourteen years absent. Ellicott finds the same two parties sitting as twenty-five years before, but will not guess how Paul told them apart: whether they sat in groups on opposite sides, after the manner of the Government and Opposition benches, or whether he recognised individual faces, there are no data for deciding. Gill notes that the proportions varied: sometimes the high priest was a Sadducee, as Ananias probably was, and sometimes the greater part or even the whole council, but this one only in part. Henry sets out what divided them. The Pharisees were bigots for ceremony, zealous not only for what God had appointed but for the tradition of the elders, yet orthodox with their church on the world of spirits, the resurrection and the life to come. The Sadducees he calls deists, who took the books of Moses for good history and good law but had little regard to the rest, denied any state of rewards or punishments beyond death, allowed no being but matter, thought God himself corporeal, and made the soul the temperament of the humours of the body.

On the tactic they divide. Robertson thinks Paul saw at once that his unwitting attack on the high priest had ruined his cause and that a fair hearing was impossible; he quotes Vincent, that Paul with great tact seeks to bring the two parties into collision, and Alford's motto, divide and conquer, while noting that Farrar condemns him outright and reads a later verse as a confession of error. Barnes calls it a master-stroke of policy evincing a profound knowledge of human nature, and reports the charges it has drawn: Orobio thought it an artful manner of declining persecution, unworthy of an upright man, and Chubb called it gross dissimulation, designed to conceal the true ground of his troubles. Calvin feels the difficulty as sharply as any critic, granting that the subtilty was inwrapped in dissimulation not far from a lie, since the strife had really arisen over the ceremonies and the admission of the Gentiles. His answer is that Paul nowhere denied being accused of other things, and said truly that the Sadducees were offended with him for holding the resurrection; the way being stopped and no place granted him to defend himself, he used the last remedy.

Whether the profession was true is another question. Chrysostom holds that Paul here discourses simply as man, not on all occasions alike enjoying supernatural aid, and speaks no falsehood, being a Pharisee by descent from his ancestors; since his accusers would not say why they arraigned him, he was compelled to declare it himself. Robertson agrees the claim was strictly true, and adds that the resurrection was the point dividing the two sects and the cardinal doctrine of his ministry, so that he was recurring to the original cleavage: the Pharisees had held aloof when the Sadducees persecuted Peter, and Gamaliel had thrown cold water on the effort to punish them. Ellicott presses the harder form of the question, whether a follower of Christ was not the sworn foe of Pharisaism, and answers that all parties have their good and bad sides. The true leaders of the Pharisees had given the resurrection a prominence it never had before and taught an ethical rather than a sacrificial religion, and there were avowed Pharisees in the Church already. Clarke reads the phrase as one thing rather than two, the hope of the resurrection, the conjunction being redundant, and traces the quarrel to its root: the apostles were imprisoned for preaching the resurrection through Jesus, because if he rose the wickedness of those who killed him was incontrovertibly established. Wesley adds that this was Paul's case in effect, though not formally or explicitly.
7:
Robertson dates the outbreak to mid-sentence, reading a genitive absolute — while he was still saying this — and notes that the word for the division, used elsewhere of insurrection, here means strife, a lively scrap that Luke pictures as going on. Ellicott judges the stroke immediately successful: it prevented the hasty unanimous vote which might otherwise have united the two parties, as they had been united in the case of Stephen, in the condemnation of a blasphemer, and what follows shows that it was not without results as regards the higher aim. Gill hears the noise of it, a loud clamour, the members beginning to talk loud and in high spirits one against another. Clarke puts the mechanics more bluntly, that the Pharisees espoused his side of the question because it stood in opposition to the Sadducees, whom they abhorred as irreligious men.

What the Sadducees denied is set out at length. Barnes makes them materialists who supposed that all the operations we ascribe to mind could be traced to some modification of matter, and cites Josephus twice: that they take away the belief of the immortal duration of the soul and the punishments and rewards in hades, and that souls die with the bodies. Robertson notes a grammatical oddity in the summary, that both is used though three items of belief have been named, an idiom common enough in the papyri. Calvin explains the reduction differently, that spirits and angels stand in one order, the souls of men and of angels being of one nature and substance, so the three points come to two. He also refuses to make the sect simple Epicureans, since they confessed that the world is governed by the providence of God and every man rewarded for his works; their error was to shut those rewards up in this life, which experience refutes, the worshippers of God being often miserably tormented while the wicked live in wealth and pleasures. Ellicott finds the position incoherent from another side. They acknowledged the Pentateuch with all its angelophanies and were more severe than others in administering the Law, and the higher priestly class were mere Sadducees, yet on their principles what did the Temple ritual mean?

The defence they were offered is judged coolly. Barnes denies that the Pharisees had become friends of Paul or of Christianity: inflamed against the Sadducees, they were willing to make use of any argument, and they perverted his statement to do it, since he had said the Lord commanded him and had said nothing of a spirit or an angel — men are not always very careful about the correctness of their statements when they wish to humble a rival. Wesley says the same more briefly, that they add nothing but construe it in their own way, putting an angel or spirit for Jesus; and Clarke notes what made that possible, since without conceding the resurrection they could allow that the soul of Christ had appeared to him. Calvin reads the scene as a warning about contention: those who detested Paul begin of a sudden to defend him, which had been well done if done with judgment, but being inflamed with hatred of their rivals they are blind in his matter. Ellicott adds a textual note, that the closing appeal not to fight against God is wanting in many of the best manuscripts and looks added to complete a sentence Luke had left in the emphasis of its unfinished abruptness, its close perhaps drowned in the tumultuous cries of the Sadducees; the line the Pharisees take is altogether Gamaliel's, and after twenty-five years they have got no further than the cautious policy of those who halt between two opinions.
10:
Gill has the quarrel come to the height where hot words were spoken and they were ready to come to blows. The verb behind the tribune's fear is violent. Robertson glosses it as to draw in two, to tear in pieces, a word used elsewhere in the New Testament of tearing chains apart, and pictures the soldiers seizing Paul out of the midst of the rabbis as they raged to get at each other; Lysias, he adds, found his prisoner more of a puzzle now than ever. Clarke explains where the rescue came from, that the chief captain was present through these transactions and had a body of soldiers held ready in the castle, whom he ordered down. Ellicott supplies the political reading. The priest who had been rebuked as a whited wall would not willingly forgo his revenge, and the Sadducees could now assume the position of being more devoted defenders of the Law and the Temple than the Pharisees themselves, while the chiliarch's alarm was heightened by knowing that he was answerable for the life of a Roman citizen. In the barracks, probably in the self-same guardroom that had witnessed our Lord's sufferings at the hands of Pilate's soldiers, the prisoner would at least be in safety. Calvin draws the moral from the riot: contention once hot has such violent motions that even most wise men are not well in their wits, and no fire is so swift, so it must be prevented at the first beginning. Yet the officer who acts only to stop an uproar is the minister of God's providence, and the Lord directs his blind hands.

On the vision that night they agree it was needed. Robertson observes that Paul had no such grip on the church as Peter, for whom the whole congregation had once prayed, so that it looked dark until Jesus spoke, and that the brave word for courage is one Jesus had used to others; the weight falls on must, and on that Paul leans. Clarke notes that he had no direct intimation how the trial would end, though he had long desired to see Rome and had some sense that he should; the vision settled every fear and scruple by telling him he would be sent there by God himself. Ellicott reconstructs the wakeful night. Personal fear of suffering or death he was more free from than most men, but was his work to be cut short, and the desire cherished for years frustrated? Such anxieties could not but find expression in his prayers, and the vision was manifestly the answer, the same word spoken to him as to the Twelve on the troubled waters of Galilee. Barnes takes the appearance itself as approval of the course he had just taken before the council, and notes that the promise was not directly one of deliverance, but implied it and made it certain.

Calvin presses what the promise withholds. The Lord does not undertake to free him, nor even say that he shall have a joyful end; he says only that the troubles which already oppress him will continue long, so that according to the flesh it had been better to die at once than to pine away in bands. That is a cold comfort until one sees what it teaches, that the Lord has respect unto us in our miseries even when he does not stretch forth his hand at once; and since oracles are no longer sent from heaven, we must meditate on the promises already given and be content with the word alone. Wesley draws the opposite lesson, that particular promises are usually given when all things appear desperate, and that a promise of what is afar off implies all that necessarily lies between: Paul shall testify at Rome, therefore he shall escape the Jews, the sea, the viper.
12:
Gill marks the hour, as soon as it was light, very early in the morning. Henry reads the plot as the third attempt on the same man. They had gained nothing by tumult or by legal process, and so had recourse to assassination; when one design fails they will turn another stone. He marks the timing too: in the night Christ appeared to protect him, and by day forty men appeared to destroy him, but they were not up so soon that Christ was not up before them. Barnes leaves the party unnamed, noting that the sacred writer does not say whether they were Sadducees, and that seeing Paul in the tribune's hands with no prospect of punishment they resolved to take the matter into their own hands; Michaelis conjectures they were of the Sicarii with which Judea then abounded. Ellicott supplies the reasoning that made such men possible. The casuistry of the more fanatic Jews concluded that a blasphemer or apostate was an outlaw, so that in the absence of any judicial condemnation private persons might execute the divine sentence upon him — as Mattathias had slain the apostate sacrificing at Modin, and as ten Zealots had conspired against Herod for building an amphitheatre in the Holy City. It is melancholy but instructive, he adds, how often Christian casuistry has run in the same groove.

The oath is examined closely. Robertson takes the word for their banding as a secret combination, a binding together like twisted cords, and pursues the verb for the curse, which Cremer and Thayer called wholly Biblical or ecclesiastical, but Deissmann quotes it from an Attic cursing tablet of Megara, which shows pagans used it as well as Jews, though he suggests Greek-speaking Jews may have coined it. Robertson also declines the past tense of the older rendering, since the sense is simply till they should kill him, and recalls that Saul's anathema once imperilled Jonathan. Ellicott identifies the form as the Jewish kherem, under which the person or thing it fell on was regarded as devoted to the wrath of God, Jericho and all it contained being the standing example. Calvin explains why such a form was chosen: there is always a secret curse in an oath, but men sometimes use express cursings to bind themselves harder, and the cause here was that it might not be lawful for them to change their purpose or call back what they had promised. Barnes adds that they might have vowed off wine or meat alone, and made the oath more binding by renouncing all food and drink.

The vow proved less binding than it sounds. Barnes reports that the Rabbins could absolve them if they were unable to execute it, and Clarke gives the ruling: he that has vowed not to eat sins against his vow if he eats and against his life if he does not, so let him go to the wise men and they will loose him, since the tongue of the wise is health. When vows were so easily dispensed with, Clarke observes, they might be readily multiplied, and Wesley says only that such vows were not uncommon and absolution an easy matter. Henry will not let the form excuse the act. To bind oneself to evil is entering into covenant with the devil and leaves no room for repentance, nay bids defiance to it, and the presumption is complete: they fixed a term as short as a fast without any reserve for the disposal of an overruling Providence, though with what face could they have inserted one? Calvin puts the usurpation in a sentence. They swear to eat nothing till Paul is slain, as if his life were in their hands, taking to themselves what God so often says is his alone; and if Satan can drive forty men headlong together, our own sluggishness in his service is the more shameful.
13:
Robertson notes that the number is given without the usual particle, a construction common in the older Greek, and that the word for the conspiracy comes from swearing together and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Gill thinks the number was the point: enough banded together to have strength sufficient to take Paul out of the soldiers' hands as he was conducted from the castle to the temple. Barnes agrees that so large a body of desperate men, bound by so solemn an oath, would be likely to succeed, and that Paul was therefore in peculiar danger. Ellicott observes which party they approached: it lies on the surface that they went to the Sadducean side of the Council, not the more moderate and cautious Pharisees, and Ananias, who had already shown the rough brutality of his nature, was now impelled by revenge. Robertson adds that they came to the Sanhedrin as Judas had, and that Jesus foretold the temper of it: whoever kills you will think that he does God service. Calvin says the priests thereby proved that there was in them neither fear of God nor humanity, for they did not merely allow the ambush but stood ready to be partners in it; and what was it to take a man out of the judge's hands and slay him, but to rage like murderers in the very place of judgment?

Ellicott gives three reasons why the murder had to be contrived rather than sentenced: the Council had lost the power of capital punishment under Rome, or if it retained it the chiliarch would never have let it be used on a Roman citizen, or the previous day had shown the violent party could not command a majority. So far the plot was skilfully laid, since even those who had said they found no evil in this man could hardly oppose a proposal for further investigation; and he hears in the pronoun opening the last clause a kind of ferocious emphasis: the council might safely leave them to do their part. Barnes measures the request by what it assumes. They knew the character of those they addressed so well that they did not doubt of success, and public justice must have been deeply fallen when such an iniquitous petition could be made with certain prospect of success; the council would not be suspected, and nothing but the interposition of Providence could have prevented so well-laid a plan. Wesley adds only that they never scrupled at it, not doubting but they were doing God service.

The nephew is the one glimpse of Paul's family in the book. Ellicott doubts that he or his mother lived in Jerusalem, since Paul lodged with Mnason, and wonders whether he was one of the kinsmen later greeted at Rome, come up for the feast and hearing the plot talked of in the caravanserai where pilgrims lodged — for it is difficult to keep a secret in which forty men are sharers. Robertson reports Vincent's guess that some Pharisee told him, Paul being of that guild, and will not decide; he does note that the young man knew what to do, had address enough to get into the barracks, and ran the risk of death if discovered. Calvin takes the turn as a lesson in providence: who would have thought a boy would disclose the lying in wait the conspirators believed known to none but themselves? Yet Paul does not sit still. Barnes remarks that he always understood the divine promises as consistent with his own efforts, and Clarke that he who will not help himself according to the power he has can look to neither reason nor revelation for assistance. Calvin puts it that he did not wait for God to stretch a hand out of heaven and work a miracle, but used the remedy offered, not doubting it was appointed by God.
18:
Ellicott lingers on the centurion's phrase. Paul the prisoner: he little thought at the time how long that name would be used of him, first by others and afterwards by himself, until it became a title of honour in which he seemed to glory almost more than in that of Apostle. Robertson describes what the word covered here — bound to a soldier, but not with the two chains of his arrest, and with enough liberty to see his friends, a military custody better than the common prison though more confining. Gill notices the officer's manner: he took the young man and brought him at once, without curiously inquiring into the thing or examining him about it, which showed a man of good disposition, ready to do a kind office even to a prisoner.

The tribune's reception of him is read the same way. Gill reports and rejects a suspicion that Lysias took the young man by the hand because he expected a present from Paul, since that represents him as a sordid and mercenary man without sufficient proof; the gesture is rather an instance of civility and good breeding, done partly out of respect to Paul and partly to encourage the young man to speak freely. Barnes adds the practical motive, that it drew him aside from the crowd so the message could be given privately. Robertson quotes Bengel on the kindly touch in Lysias, and notes that the word for the youth is the one used of Paul himself at Stephen's death, so that he was probably in his twenties, and that the imperfect means the tribune began questioning him. Wesley thinks the whole affair was conducted with great integrity, humanity and prudence. Calvin will not leave it at natural courtesy. A man trained up in the wars might as easily have repulsed a stranger as despised Paul's suit, so this must be ascribed to the grace of God, who promised to give his people favour in the sight of the Egyptians and who mollifies hard hearts and tames fierce spirits when he means to use men as helps to his own. Those in authority may learn from it what a great virtue courtesy is, since had access been difficult he might through ignorance have delivered Paul to be killed; magistrates often fall into great offences through pride, because they will not admit those who would give them good counsel.

How the nephew came by his news is left open. Barnes can only conjecture that he was a student under one of the Jewish teachers, and observes that the forty were not very careful about concealment, having told the whole oath to the chief priests and elders. Robertson notes that the youth repeats the conspirators' own words, as though he had overheard them, and that he says the Jews as if the whole nation were in it, though the men were more probably Zealots; when he speaks of the inquiry he puts it in the singular, out of deference to the tribune's authority, which softens the scheming a little, and Page is wrong to call the phrase absurd. The last clause Robertson thinks the shrewdest thing in the speech, since the promise from Lysias is the one item needed to put the plot through. Gill defends the boldness of the advice, which is not to be imputed to pride or vanity in a young man directing the chief captain, but to his great affection for his uncle, which moved him to entreat rather than direct. Ellicott finds Lysias plainly glad of the intelligence, his sympathies with Paul against the high priest and his followers, welcoming a chance to show zeal for the safe-keeping of a Roman citizen and to state the whole transaction from his own point of view; and with true official caution he treats what he has heard as confidential and takes his measures accordingly.
23:
Robertson counts three arms in the order, the three varieties of troops in a Roman army: the heavy-armed legionaries, the horsemen that belonged to every legion, and a light-armed supplementary force whose name means those who take with the right hand. He also reads the two centurions as some two, which Page took to mean they were not specially chosen. The third term is the difficulty. Barnes says it is found nowhere else in the New Testament and in no classical writer, that it properly means those who apprehend by the right hand, and that some would emend it to a word meaning those who cast with the right hand, which is how the Vulgate, the Syriac and the Arabic take it; Clarke notes that the Alexandrian manuscript actually reads the second form, and thinks the two come to nearly the same thing. Ellicott treats it as a strictly technical term for light troops carrying a javelin in one hand, as against those whose older spear had a shaft too heavy to be wielded but with both, and observes that the military writers of the Byzantine empire couple them with archers and light shield-bearers.

The escort seems large for one prisoner, and both note it. Ellicott says the tumults of the previous days and the information just received gave the chiliarch good reason to apprehend a formidable attack, and that his object was plainly to get the prisoner beyond reach before daybreak, which is why all were to be mounted. Barnes reckons the whole detail at nearly five hundred men, and justifies it twice over: the conspirators were themselves numerous, and they were men accustomed to scenes of blood, of desperate characters, who had sworn away his life, so the guard was made strong enough to deter them from attempting it. He distinguishes the parts of it, too — the foot were meant only to see Paul safely out of Jerusalem, while the horsemen went the whole way to Caesarea. On the hour they agree: the third of the night is about nine in the evening, and Clarke says the time was chosen for the greater secrecy, to elude the cunning and active malice of the Jews.

Gill notes that the Syriac reads a beast in the singular, one being sufficient for Paul, while the Arabic and Ethiopic leave the clause out. Robertson explains why beasts were wanted at all. Paul was chained to a soldier, so another animal would be needed for the baggage, and seventy miles might require a change of horses; they were riding animals or pack animals, asses or horses, but not war-horses. He adds that some Latin manuscripts account for the extreme precaution of Lysias by his fear of a night attack, which might leave him open to a charge of bribery before Felix, and thinks Luke probably travelled with Paul. Wesley remarks only that this is the one time we read of his riding, and not by choice. On the governor himself the accounts converge. Ellicott sets him in the household of Antonia, the mother of Claudius, where he and his brother Pallas were first slaves and then freedmen, and where Pallas rose to be the emperor's favourite minister and got his brother the procuratorship; Barnes and Robertson add that he held it until complaints to Nero brought Festus in his place. Tacitus supplies the verdict all of them quote, that he wielded the power of a king in the temper of a slave, and Robertson calls him one of the most depraved men of his time. Ellicott counts from Suetonius the three queens he married in succession, the second of them Drusilla, who had left Azizus king of Emesa for him, and whose son by him died in the eruption of Vesuvius.
25:
Robertson explains why such a letter existed at all: Roman law required a subordinate officer reporting a case to his superior to send a written statement of it. He sees no reason to doubt that what Luke gives is a genuine copy, since the letter may well have been read out in open court before Felix, since Luke was probably with Paul, and since a copy may have reached Paul after his appeal; it was probably written in Latin. Clarke goes further and takes this to be not merely the substance but the letter itself, the whole being so perfectly formal, in just the manner of all ancient letters, that he counts it another proof of Luke's accuracy. Ellicott allows either that it was sent unsealed or that a copy reached Paul or Luke afterwards, and finds in it the obvious marks of a verbal reproduction. Gill takes the writer's name apart: the first is Roman and may have been assumed from the Emperor Claudius, since the man was not born a Roman, while the second is Greek and was his proper name, so that he was likely a Greek who had bought his freedom with money.

The formulas are conventional and worth placing. Ellicott notes that the epithet rendered most excellent is the one Luke uses of Theophilus at the head of his Gospel, and that the bare greeting matches the letter of the Council at Jerusalem and the opening of the Epistle of James. Barnes calls the address a mere title of office, and notes that Paul's life had already been twice endangered in the way described. Robertson adds that the first is the usual style for men of rank, answering to Your Excellency, and that the second is an absolute infinitive standing with an absolute nominative, the form of countless papyrus letters. Calvin fills in who the recipient was. Felix was brother to Pallas, a freedman of Caesar who came to equal the chief men of the city in wealth and power, and on whom the senate bestowed the ornaments of the praetor with titles of filthy and shameful flattery; since the servants of Claudius abused his folly and ruled the empire at their pleasure, it is no marvel that Pallas made his brother governor of Judaea. The letter's aim, on Calvin's reading, is to help Paul by the tribune's own prior verdict, and to discredit his adversaries so that they may not be able to hurt him.

What the letter leaves out is noticed by all who read it closely. Ellicott says the chief captain ingeniously colours his statement so as to claim credit for having rescued a Roman citizen, when in fact he did not discover the citizenship until he was on the point of scourging Paul without a trial, and that fact is passed over without a word. Robertson is blunter. Wendt, Zoeckler and Furneaux try to defend the reversal of the two facts from being an actual lie, which Bengel rightly says it is, and the grammar gives them no help, since Greek has no aorist participle of subsequent action; Lysias reversed the order and dropped the order to scourge, to stand well with his superior and pose as the protector of a fellow citizen. Furneaux's summary, that the whole is a dexterous mixture of truth and falsehood, Robertson thinks carries its own stamp of genuineness. Calvin does not defend the writer either, but looks past him: the commendation was not purchased by prayer or flattery or bought with money, so how came a soldier to be so courteous, freely, to an obscure man whom all men hated, unless the Lord had appointed him to be his servant's patron? Henry says the same more broadly, that God has instruments for every work, and that the natural abilities and moral virtues of the heathen have often been employed to protect his persecuted servants.
28:
Robertson hears the tribune's frustration in the tenses. The verb for learning the charge means to know fully, and the imperfect that follows says the accusers were accusing him, repeating their charges rather than stating one. Gill guesses what those charges sounded like to a Roman ear: questions about the resurrection of the dead and a future state, which some in the council denied and others asserted, must have seemed idle and foolish to a heathen, and the popular outcry about defiling the temple and speaking contemptibly of the law and the holy place concerned things the captain knew little of. Ellicott reconstructs the residue more exactly, as three points that would have presented themselves to the chiliarch after his inquiries: that the prisoner was accused of transgressing the rules of the Temple, that the issue seemed to turn on whether he had seen a teacher named Jesus risen from the dead, and whether that teacher was entitled to the name of Christ.

The verdict in the letter matters more than the confusion in it. Robertson observes that the distinction drawn is the very one Gallio had drawn at Corinth, and that Lysias is here expressing the opinion that Paul ought to be set free; the lenient treatment Paul afterwards received at Caesarea and at Rome probably owes something to this report, and it belongs to a pattern, since every Roman magistrate before whom he appears declares him innocent. Barnes states the finding plainly, that Paul had done nothing worthy of death or of bonds by the Roman law, having committed no crime against the Roman people. Calvin accepts the acquittal so far as the man's judgment could reach, but will not let it pass as a principle, because it is a profane man who speaks. Among the people of God, corrupting the doctrine of godliness with false opinions deserves no less punishment than wronging men; the Romans would never have suffered their own worships to be plucked up, and it was only because they made no account of the law of God that troubling the Church with false opinions counted as no fault, which is why their law forbade governors to meddle in such matters. Nothing is more absurd, he adds, than that theft should be punished while those who rob God of his honour escape.

The referral itself is straightforward. Clarke takes Felix to be the proper person before whom the business should ultimately come and be decided, and glosses the closing word as a wish for good health. Ellicott notes that this formula, like the opening one, agrees with the letter of the Council at Jerusalem, and suspects that the order sending the accusers down to Caesarea answered the high priest's request for another inquiry before the Sanhedrin. Two loose ends are left. Ellicott supposes the forty considered themselves absolved from their vow as soon as they heard the prisoner was gone, so that the fast probably lasted no more than eighteen or twenty hours; Robertson says only that we have no way of knowing, and that neither they nor the Jews from Asia are heard of again through the five years of imprisonment that followed. Calvin reads the last paragraph of the letter as the tribune turning their hatred back on the accusers: had they persecuted Paul lawfully they would have trusted the goodness of their cause and let him be judged according to law, and their willingness to kill him privately shows they had no case.
31:
Chrysostom sees the escort as an unintended honour: like some king whom his body-guards escort, so did these convey Paul, in such numbers too, and by night, for fear of the wrath of the people. He draws the tribune's own opinion out of the arrangements, since Lysias would not have sent him off with such care for his safety but that, having found nothing amiss in him, he knew the murderous disposition of his adversaries. Robertson reads the phrase as according to that which was commanded them, and calls the stage a hard night's ride, forty miles through the dark. Wesley doubts they did it in one, since Antipatris lay some thirty-eight of our miles north-west of Jerusalem and Caesarea nearly seventy from the city. Clarke presses the same point grammatically: we need not suppose the whole troop reached the town on the night they left, and the sentence may be read simply as the soldiers taking Paul by night and bringing him to Antipatris.

The town is placed carefully. Barnes and Clarke agree it was anciently Capharsaba, that Herod the Great rebuilt it and named it for his father Antipater, and that it lay on the road from Jerusalem to Caesarea; Barnes adds that it stood in a fine plain, watered with many springs and fountains, while Clarke connects the older name with the Capharsalama of the Maccabees. Ellicott identifies it with the modern Kefr-Saba, puts it forty-two miles from Jerusalem and twenty-six from Caesarea, and reports traces of a Roman road running between it and Jerusalem more directly, by some miles, than the better known route through the pass of Beth-horon; starting about midnight they would arrive around six or seven in the morning. From there the escort was halved. Gill counts the four hundred on foot turning back and leaving the seventy horsemen to finish, all danger from the Jews being over once Antipatris was reached, and Ellicott has the infantry return to their barracks in the Tower Antonia as no longer needed. Calvin adds the tribune's reasoning: once some part of the journey was finished the adversaries could have no hope of overtaking them, and it was no point of wisdom to send part of the garrison far away.

Robertson marks the arrival with an irony. The cavalry handed over the letter and presented Paul, and one wonders what his friends in Caesarea, Philip and his daughters, thought of the prophecy of Agabus now so quickly come true. Gill credits the governor with care and diligence for reading the letter at once, not knowing what important business it might contain. The question Felix then asks is procedural. Barnes takes it as an attempt to ascertain whether the prisoner properly belonged to his jurisdiction, noting that how far that jurisdiction extended is not certainly known, though it appears to have included Cilicia. Robertson makes the question sharper still, since the word means of what kind of province, whether senatorial or imperial; Cilicia, like Judaea, lay under the propraetor of Syria, and the arrest having been made in Jerusalem the case was Felix's unless it turned out to be a matter of insurrection. Ellicott finds the readiness to hear it more puzzling than the question, since by the precedent Pilate set the case belonged elsewhere; perhaps Felix had no motive for conciliating the governor of Cilicia, or judged that the nature of the accusation over-ruled the nationality of the accused. Chrysostom notes what the adjournment costs Paul: Lysias has already spoken for his exculpation, and now the accusers will have the chance to gain the hearer beforehand.
35:
The verb of the promise is stronger than it looks. Robertson renders it I will hear thee fully, and reads what follows as an indefinite clause, whenever thine accusers come; Ellicott says the Greek expresses the idea of a thorough hearing, and Clarke expands it into a fair, full and attentive hearing in the presence of the accusers, where the prisoner shall be permitted to defend himself. Gill catches a courtly note in the Arabic and Ethiopic, which read we will hear. The place of custody is disputed only in emphasis. Barnes explains that the word once meant the tent of the Roman praetor, and because justice was administered there came to be applied to halls or courts of justice, this one having probably been reared by Herod the Great, with places of security attached as such buildings usually had. Ellicott thinks judgment hall hardly gives the sense, the term ranging from a palace to a barrack: the building was probably meant by Herod for a royal residence and was now used by the procurator for himself and his troops, so that the Apostle had here a second experience of the life of a praetorium. Wesley supposes some tower belonging to it served as a kind of state prison, and Robertson traces the word from the general's camp to the governor's palace and finally to the praetorian guard.

Clarke closes the chapter with a series of reflections. The first is on the plea Paul opened with: conscience is generally allowed to be the rule of human actions, but it cannot be a right rule unless it be well informed, and while unenlightened it may guide its professor to perdition and cause the ruin of others, so that an ill-informed conscience may burn even the saints for God's sake. The second is on the rebuke he accepted: no circumstance in which a man can be placed excuses him from showing reverence to the authorities providence has instituted, since an evil can never be of use and a good may be abused, yet does not lose its essential qualities by the abuse. The third is on the stroke that divided the council, which he allows so long as truth itself is not violated and error is exposed by it; and he adds that God frequently raises up defenders of the principles of truth even among those who in practice are its decided enemies, one such having fostered the principles by which error was banished from these lands.

The last of his observations answers a question the chapter raises. If Paul had Christ's own assurance that he should see Rome, why did he not sit still when his nephew brought word of the ambush? Because God makes use of the prudence with which he has endowed man as an agent in that very providence by which he supports him, and to neglect the natural means of safety is to tempt and dishonour him, and may induce him to use in judgment what he had designed for our comfort; prudence, Clarke concludes, is well associated even with an apostolical spirit. He sets the two designs side by side. In the generality of human events we do not often distinguish the purposes of God from those of men, and here the design of Lysias was to keep his own conduct free from exception, while the design of God was to bring Paul safely to Rome, that he might attack idolatry in its strongest fort. Felix he credits with one piece of wisdom, in refusing to hear the case until the accusers stood face to face with the accused, since to hear one side separately makes the evil seem very great. Ellicott looks further ahead, noting that at Rome the Apostle does not appear to have been lodged in the praetorium, though the circumstances of that imprisonment brought him into contact with the soldiers quartered there.
